title: Complexity
body:
**In this course, "complexity" means *software* complexity: how hard a system is to
understand and change.** It is not [[Time Complexity]] (how an algorithm's running time
scales) and it is not [[NP-Complete|computational complexity]] (which problems are tractable
at all). Same word, three different subjects, and the vault has all three. An algorithm can
be $O(n \log n)$ and still be unreadable; a piece of code can be trivially $O(n)$ and still
be the worst file in the project.

## What makes software complex

The number of things you have to hold in your head to change one line safely. That comes from:

- **Interactions between modules**, not the size of any one module. A 10,000-line system of
  independent parts is easier than a 2,000-line system where everything calls everything.
  This is [[Coupling and Cohesion]] and it is the dominant term.
- **Branching within a function.** Each `if` doubles the paths through the code. Counting
  those paths is the standard product [[Metrics|metric]] for it.
- **Scale.** Interactions grow faster than parts do, which is why "just write it carefully"
  stops working at some size and process ([[SDLC]], [[Review]], [[Unit testing]]) has to take
  over.

## Essential and accidental

The distinction worth keeping. **Essential** complexity is in the problem: payroll has tax
rules, and no design removes them. **Accidental** complexity is what the solution added:
tangled dependencies, a framework that fights the problem, five ways to do the same thing.
Design work only ever attacks the second kind, and confusing them leads to rewrites that
rediscover the same difficulty in a new shape.

Complexity is why the field has [[Models]], [[Abstraction]], and [[Paradigms]] at all. See
[[Design]] and [[Code Smells]].
